title: Blind Spot Detection with FMCW Radar and ADALM Pluto SDR
summary: A proof-of-concept FMCW radar built on the ADALM Pluto software-defined radio that detects multiple objects and estimates how far away each one is — the core sensing behind vehicle blind-spot detection.
overview: Blind-spot detection systems warn drivers about vehicles they can't see in their mirrors. For my final-year capstone, I built a proof-of-concept of the sensing side of that problem: an FMCW radar on low-cost ADALM Pluto SDR hardware that detects multiple objects in a controlled environment and estimates the distance to each one.

sections.heading: How FMCW radar measures distance
text: An FMCW (frequency-modulated continuous-wave) radar transmits a “chirp” — a signal whose frequency sweeps steadily over time. When the chirp reflects off an object and comes back, it arrives slightly late, so at any instant the received signal is at a different frequency from the one being sent.
That frequency difference grows with the object's distance. Measuring it turns a timing problem into a frequency problem, which is much easier to solve with signal processing.

image.caption: Transmitted vs. received chirp — the gap between them reveals distance.

sections.heading: Building it on the ADALM Pluto SDR
sections.text: The ADALM Pluto is a small, affordable software-defined radio. I used it as the radar's transmitter and receiver, with the signal generation and processing written in MATLAB.
bullets: Developed a proof-of-concept FMCW radar detection system on ADALM Pluto SDR hardware.
Implemented distance estimation algorithms by analyzing the frequency difference between transmitted and received signals.
Applied signal processing techniques to extract meaningful data from the received radar signals.

image.caption: ADALM Pluto SDR and antenna setup.

sections.heading: Testing in a controlled environment
sections.text: To understand how well the system really works, I designed and ran controlled experiments that evaluated:
bullets: Accuracy: how close the estimated distances are to the true distances.
Resolution: how close together two objects can be and still be told apart.
Multi-object detection: detecting and ranging several objects at once.
Material sensitivity: how different materials affect the reflected signal.

title: Smart Irrigation System
summary: An automated irrigation prototype that adjusts watering based on soil moisture and humidity — shaped by interviews with 15 farmers and agricultural experts.
overview: Watering on a fixed schedule wastes water when the soil is already moist and falls short when conditions change. This community-based project makes irrigation respond to what the field actually needs: a prototype that reads soil moisture and humidity and adjusts watering automatically, designed to improve water efficiency and automation in agriculture.

sections.heading: Starting with the people who'd use it
sections.text: Before choosing any hardware, I conducted user research with 15 farmers and agricultural experts to understand the real-world irrigation challenges they face and what a useful system would need to do. Those conversations shaped the system's requirements.

image.caption: Talking with farmers about their irrigation challenges.

sections.heading: Designing the system
bullets: Integrated sensors, microcontrollers, and actuators into an automated irrigation control system.
Researched and selected appropriate electronic components and communication protocols for reliable operation.
Designed the system to adjust watering automatically based on soil moisture and humidity levels.

sections.text: The working prototype brings sensing, control, and actuation together in one automated system that waters only when the readings show it's needed.

title: DC–DC Converter for EV Solar Charging Station
summary: Led a team of six to design and simulate a DC–DC converter for a solar-powered EV charging station concept — from business plan to circuit simulation.
overview: A solar charging station has to turn the power coming from its panels into the voltage an electric vehicle needs. A DC–DC converter does that job. I led a team of six students to design one for an EV solar charging station concept, covering both the engineering and the business case.

sections.heading: Leading the team
sections.text: As team lead, I contributed to both the technical design and project management, coordinating six people across engineering, documentation, and business work.
bullets: Developed a business plan and a product concept report.
Wrote the technical specifications for the converter.

sections.heading: Design & simulation
sections.text: We designed the converter circuit and simulated it in MATLAB and LTSpice to check how it behaves before any hardware is built.
